title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Mohs surgeons should be knowledgeable in both nonsurgical treatments for nonmelanoma skin cancers (NMSCs) and preventive strategies for high-risk patients. Individuals with immunosuppression, extensive sun exposure, or genetic predispositions may benefit from chemoprophylaxis to reduce morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs associated with NMSCs, particularly basal cell carcinoma (BCC) and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Nicotinamide and oral retinoids are medications used in NMSC prophylaxis. Nicotinamide and retinoids are derivatives of vitamin B3 and vitamin A, respectively. These agents can cause systemic adverse effects, including teratogenicity, mucocutaneous dryness, hepatotoxicity, and mood disturbances. Careful monitoring and patient counseling are essential. For patients unable to tolerate systemic agents, alternative chemoprophylactic options include topical therapies (eg, 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod) and photodynamic therapy. Coordination with transplant teams may be necessary, as modifying immunosuppressive regimens can also reduce skin cancer risk.

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity reviews the benefits, limitations, and risks of each agent, allowing Mohs surgeons to individualize treatment and improve patient outcomes. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying the indications, mechanisms of action, contraindications, and adverse event profiles for nicotinamide and oral retinoids as chemoprophylactic agents for nonmelanoma skin cancer and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when administering these therapies.

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Determine the mechanism of action of chemoprophylactic agents such as nicotinamide and oral retinoids in patients at increased risk of nonmelanoma skin cancer. Select appropriate candidates for chemoprophylaxis with nicotinamide and oral retinoids in patients at increased risk of nonmelanoma skin cancer. Implement best practices for managing the adverse effects of nicotinamide and oral retinoids in patients undergoing chemotherapeutic treatment for nonmelanoma skin cancer. Apply interprofessional team strategies to improve outcomes for solid-organ transplant recipients requiring chemoprophylaxis against nonmelanoma skin cancer. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic.

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Introduction
content: The Mohs surgeon should be familiar with nonsurgical options for treating nonmelanoma skin cancers (NMSCs) and medical options for preventing the formation of new skin cancers. Patients not well-suited for cutaneous surgery due to their overall clinical health can be offered alternative treatment modalities such as topical or systemic chemotherapy or radiation. Patients with extensive sun exposure over the years, certain genodermatoses, chronic radiation exposure, and immunosuppression are at a greater risk of developing NMSCs than those without these risk factors. [1] In patients with increased risk factors, chemoprophylaxis, or agents used to slow the growth of NMSCs, can be utilized to prevent the formation of NMSCs and, subsequently, the associated morbidity and mortality. [1]

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Introduction
content: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most prevalent NMSC in the United States, with an annual incidence of approximately 2 million. [2] Although death from BCC is rare, the tumors can be associated with significant morbidity and cost. The second most common NMSC, squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), has an annual incidence of approximately 700,000 cases in the United States, of which approximately 2% result in death. [3] In addition to preventing the morbidity and mortality associated with these NMSCs, evidence suggests that preventive measures, such as chemoprophylaxis, can save the healthcare system money. A 2015 study analyzed the economic burden of skin cancer treatments and found that the average annual cost of these treatments increased from $3.6 billion in 2002 to 2006 and from $ 8.1 billion in 2007 to 2011. [4] Preventing new NMSC formation can reduce healthcare expenditures and improve patient outcomes, including morbidity and mortality.

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Introduction
content: Nicotinamide and oral retinoids are 2 systemic chemopreventive medications used in populations at high risk of developing NMSCs. A survey sent to the American College of Mohs Surgeons found that 76.9% of the respondents recommend nicotinamide to their patients for NMSC prevention. [5] These 2 medications are essential tools the Mohs surgeon can utilize to decrease morbidity and mortality in patients with multiple NMSCs.

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Function -- Nicotinamide
content: Nicotinamide is a form of water-soluble vitamin B3 available in both oral and topical formulations. The oral formulation has been demonstrated to decrease the rate of NMSC formation. [6]

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Function -- Nicotinamide
content: Nicotinamide plays a crucial role in glycolysis by generating the NAD+ required for ATP production and is therefore critical to cellular energy generation and influencing cellular metabolism. [7] By preventing cellular energy depletion, nicotinamide enhances excisional DNA repair and prevents immunosuppression caused by ultraviolet radiation (UVR). [1]

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Function -- Nicotinamide
content: Recommendations have been published in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology (JAAD) that support using nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily in patients with field cancerization or a history of more than 1 SCC. [8] [9] These recommendations are based on a randomized controlled trial in Australia that enrolled immunocompetent patients with more than 2 NMSCs into a nicotinamide arm and a placebo arm. This trial found a 23% decrease in SCCs and a 13% reduction in actinic keratoses (AKs) in patients taking nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily, followed over 1 year, compared to the patients taking a placebo. [10] This study did not find a significant decrease in new BCC formation in the nicotinamide group compared to the placebo group. [10]

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Function -- Nicotinamide
content: The same research group investigated the use of nicotinamide in renal transplant recipients; however, this study was underpowered to assess the rate of SCC formation in this patient population. [11] A different research group published a randomized placebo-controlled trial in March 2023 that found that oral nicotinamide therapy over 1 year did not decrease NMSCs or AKs in immunosuppressed solid-organ transplant recipients. [12] Furthermore, a systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to assess the effect of nicotinamide on skin cancer prophylaxis, regardless of immunosuppression status. This analysis found moderate-quality evidence to support the use of nicotinamide for SCC prevention and low-quality evidence to support its use for BCC prevention in general and among organ-transplant recipient populations. [13]

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Function -- Retinoids
content: Retinoids comprise both natural and synthetic vitamin A analogs, with multiple therapeutic uses in dermatology, including the treatment of acne, psoriasis, and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Numerous topical and oral formulations of retinoids target retinoid nuclear receptors to exert their effects. The mechanism of action regarding retinoid chemoprophylaxis is poorly understood but likely represents a combination of factors, including immunomodulation, inhibition of cellular proliferation and keratinization, and induction of apoptosis. [14]

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Function -- Retinoids
content: The third-generation oral retinoid, acitretin, is well-established in the literature as a preventive measure for skin cancer formation in solid-organ transplant recipients and patients with diseases that predispose them to UVR damage, eg, xeroderma pigmentosum. Isotretinoin, a first-generation oral retinoid, has a single documented case of its use in a kidney-transplant recipient. This patient was treated with 0.5 mg to 1.0 mg/kg/day, resulting in a subsequent reduction of new NMSCs by approximately half over a 2-month period. [15] Although the use of isotretinoin in the transplant population is not well studied, it may be considered an alternative in patients who cannot tolerate acitretin due to renal insufficiency. [16] Isotretinoin has also been shown to decrease the incidence of NMSC in patients with xeroderma pigmentosum. Treatment with isotretinoin 2 mg/kg/day in these patients over 2 years resulted in a 63% decrease in NMSC formation in 5 of 7 patients. [17] [18]

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Function -- Retinoids
content: Limited evidence has demonstrated the use of other oral retinoids in the chemoprevention of NMSCs. Oral alitretinoin is not commercially available in the United States and is primarily used for the treatment of chronic eczema in Europe. [19] Bexarotene is primarily used to treat cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and has been used in lymphoproliferative disorders in organ transplant recipients. [20] [21]

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Function -- Retinoids
content: A 2018 study recommends starting a patient on prophylactic acitretin if a patient has developed more than 5 SCCs over 2 to 3 years, the formation of at least 1 SCC of stage T2b/T3 or higher in combination with field photodamage, or field photodamage that is nonresponsive to 5-fluorouracil or photodynamic therapy. [9] In these patient populations, the authors recommend starting oral acitretin at 10 mg every other day with gradual dose increases as tolerated over a month until a final dose of 20 mg daily is reached. [9]

content: The adverse effects of the chemoprophylactic agents should be weighed against their potential benefit to patients.

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Issues of Concern -- Nicotinamide adverse effects
content: Nicotinamide is a form of water-soluble vitamin B3 and, therefore, a relatively safe medication; excess nicotinamide is readily excreted from the body. However, patients should be counseled to avoid the readily available over-the-counter formulation of niacin, as it can cause flushing. [22] Over-the-counter formulations of nicotinamide are available that can help mitigate this effect. Additionally, nicotinamide can result in liver failure at doses greater than 3 g daily. [23]

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Issues of Concern -- Adverse effects of topical  and oral retinoids
content: Topical retinoids primarily have localized adverse effects, including redness, dryness, pruritus, and skin peeling. [24] The adverse effects of oral retinoids are more systemic and potentially more severe than those of topical retinoids. Oral retinoid therapy is teratogenic, affecting the developing fetal central nervous system, cardiovascular system, thymus, and face. [24] Although topical retinoid formulations do not appear to concentrate in plasma, even when used in doses exceeding the recommended amount, many practitioners still advise against using topical retinoids during pregnancy. [25] The potential teratogenic effects of retinoids used as chemoprophylaxis may be a lesser concern overall, as most patients requiring chemoprophylaxis are beyond childbearing age. However, it could still be relevant for a small subset of patients.

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Issues of Concern -- Adverse effects of topical  and oral retinoids
content: Other effects of oral retinoids include dryness of mucous membranes, arthralgias, myalgias, bone pain, headaches, and night blindness. [24] Dryness of the mucous membranes, especially cheilitis, is common and is typically treated symptomatically. Evidence suggests that retinoids impact bone metabolism; however, studies are conflicting on whether these drugs decrease bone mineral density over time. However, skeletal hyperostosis and extraspinal calcification of ligaments and tendons can occur with the use of oral retinoids. [26] Headaches associated with oral retinoids tend to be mild; however, a high index of suspicion is warranted for pseudotumor cerebri if the headaches are severe and accompanied by visual symptoms. Additionally, concurrent use of retinoids and tetracyclines should be avoided since this class of drugs is also associated with pseudotumor cerebri. [27]

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Issues of Concern -- Adverse effects of topical  and oral retinoids
content: Oral retinoids are also associated with elevated cholesterol, triglycerides, and liver enzymes. [24] The liver enzyme elevations typically peak between 2 and 8 weeks of therapy and then return to baseline. Current laboratory screening recommendations include baseline screening of complete blood count, creatinine, lipid panel, and liver enzymes. A lipid panel and liver enzymes should be checked monthly for 1 to 2 months after therapy initiation, as the dose is escalated, and then every 3 months once the patient has reached a stable dose. [24] [9] A meta-analysis found that isotretinoin causes an increase in both lipids and liver enzymes; however, the mean changes were not considered high-risk. [28] If liver enzymes increase more than 3-fold above the upper limit of normal, discontinuing the oral retinoid is advised. [29] Alcohol use should be strongly discouraged in patients taking oral retinoids due to an associated increase in retinoid metabolism and subsequent hepatic toxicity and fibrosis. [30]

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Issues of Concern -- Adverse effects of topical  and oral retinoids
content: Depression is an effect of oral retinoids that remains debated. Some literature suggests an association between oral retinoids and mood disorders; other sources indicate improved mood while on the medication, possibly due to improvement in the underlying cutaneous condition. [31] Patients undergoing oral retinoid therapy should be screened for depression and mood disorders and counseled about the possible association; the medication should be discontinued if symptoms arise during oral retinoid therapy. [24]

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Issues of Concern -- Adverse effects of topical  and oral retinoids
content: Acitretin has been associated with poor wound healing, characterized by excessive granulation tissue formation and the development of hypertrophic scarring. A study published in 2004 evaluating the surgical outcomes of solid-organ transplant patients taking acitretin did not find a significant difference in wound healing complications when compared to patients not taking the medication. [32]

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Clinical Significance
content: Patients most likely to require chemoprophylaxis for NMSCs include transplant recipients on immunosuppressive medications, individuals with certain genodermatoses, and those with a history of significant sun exposure throughout their lifetime. Since Mohs surgeons are likely to encounter more aggressive NMSCs in practice, they should be familiar with the risks unique to each of these populations and the appropriate management of NMSC chemoprophylaxis.

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Clinical Significance
content: According to the United Network for Organ Sharing, more than 42,800 organ transplants were performed in 2022. Solid-organ transplant recipients are estimated to have between 60 and 250 times the risk of developing an SCC and 10 to 40 times the risk of developing a BCC compared to the general population. [33] An estimated 3% of  NMSCs cause cancer-related deaths in the transplant population. [34] Most skin cancers will begin to develop within 8 years of transplant in younger patients, but as early as 3 years in patients who undergo transplant after age 60. [35] [36] Furthermore, the time interval between the formation of new skin cancers reduces with each subsequent occurrence following the appearance of the initial skin cancer. Additionally, the severity of the tumors correlates with the total number of skin cancers the patient has experienced. [37] SCCs also tend to be more aggressive in transplant recipients, with a recurrence rate of 13.4%. [38]

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Clinical Significance
content: The most important factor in NMSC development in this patient population is high UVR exposure before and after the transplant. [39] [33] Other predisposing factors to NMSC development include fair skin, aging, tobacco use, and infection with the Human papillomavirus. [33] These factors must be considered when evaluating the risk of NMSC in solid-organ transplant patients and the timing of the initiation of chemoprophylaxis therapy.

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Other Issues
content: Patients should be informed that discontinuing acitretin will rapidly return the rate of SCC formation to its baseline level. [40] Other potential chemoprophylaxis measures can be considered if acitretin is contraindicated or poorly tolerated. Other chemoprophylactic options include photodynamic therapy or topical chemoprophylaxis with retinoids, 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod, or diclofenac. Of these options, 5-fluorouracil and imiquimod have the strongest level of evidence for use. [9]

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Other Issues
content: The role of nicotinamide as a chemoprophylactic agent for melanocytic tumors appears plausible based on its mechanism of action; however, it has not been confirmed in clinical trials. [41] However, some evidence suggests that administering N-acetylcysteine may reduce ultraviolet-induced oxidative stress in melanocytic nevi, thereby reducing the long-term risk of melanoma. [42]

content: Studies have well established that switching from a calcineurin inhibitor to a mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitor reduces the number of NMSCs seen in both kidney and liver transplant recipients. [43] Communicating with the transplant physician and making appropriate drug regimen modification recommendations is essential, especially if the patient has experienced multiple or high-risk NMSCs.

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Although some Mohs surgeons will not medically manage high-risk patients, they must understand which patients may benefit from chemoprophylaxis and work with the primary dermatologist to ensure they receive comprehensive care. Additionally, if the Mohs surgeon does manage high-risk patients with chemoprophylaxis, they should work alongside the transplant physician to ensure their medication regimen balances the role of organ anti-rejection and the development of malignancies. Several prospective randomized controlled trials have demonstrated that mTOR inhibitors, such as sirolimus, reduce the incidence of SCCs in the organ transplant population. [44] [45] [46]

title: Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Chemoprophylaxis Options for Nicotinamide and Oral Retinoids  -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Collaboration among healthcare professionals involved in the care of solid-organ transplant recipients should also include nurses and pharmacists. An interprofessional approach ensures comprehensive care, sharing of expertise, and better management of potential complications. By implementing these strategies, the healthcare team can help reduce the risk of developing skin cancer in patients who have undergone solid-organ transplantation. Early detection, sun protection, regular monitoring, and comprehensive care are essential for promoting the best possible outcomes and overall well-being in these patients.
